name: Neutron-star superfluids and superconducting protons
summary: The same gap equation predicts 1S0 neutron superfluidity in the crust, 3P2 neutron pairing and type-II proton superconductivity with flux tubes in the core; these set neutron-star cooling (pair-breaking neutrino emission), specific heat and rotational dynamics. Dilute neutron matter is close to the unitary Fermi gas.
breaks: Gaps are not measured directly and depend strongly on medium polarization and three-nucleon forces; the protons sit in a neutron superfluid with entrainment, a coupling absent in metals.
sources: Baym, Pethick & Pines (1969). "Superfluidity in Neutron Stars". *Nature* 224, 673. [doi:10.1038/224673a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/224673a0)
Dean & Hjorth-Jensen (2003). "Pairing in nuclear systems: from neutron stars to finite nuclei". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 607. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.607](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.607)
Gezerlis & Carlson (2008). "Strongly paired fermions: Cold atoms and neutron matter". *Phys. Rev. C* 77, 032801. [arXiv:0711.3006](https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.3006)

name: Pulsar glitches as vortex pinning and creep
summary: Glitches are explained by quantized neutron-superfluid vortices pinned to crust nuclei that unpin collectively, and post-glitch relaxation by thermally activated vortex creep: the Anderson-Kim flux-creep physics of type-II superconductors, carried to neutron stars by Anderson himself.
breaks: Neutron vortices are neutral (no flux, no Lorentz force); pinning energies and whether the crustal superfluid can store enough angular momentum (the entrainment problem) are disputed.
sources: Anderson & Itoh (1975). "Pulsar glitches and restlessness as a hard superfluidity phenomenon". *Nature* 256, 25. [doi:10.1038/256025a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/256025a0)
Chamel & Haensel (2008). "Physics of Neutron Star Crusts". *Living Rev. Relativ.* 11, 10. [arXiv:0812.3955](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.3955)

name: 3P2 neutron superfluid as triplet p-wave pairing
summary: Spin-triplet 3P2 neutron pairing in neutron-star cores has an anisotropic, multicomponent order parameter like superfluid 3He and the p-wave pairing behind topological superconductors, which raises the question of protected surface modes and half-quantum vortices in neutron stars.
breaks: The 3P2 channel is driven by the tensor and spin-orbit forces with L=1, S=1, J=2 rather than pure p-wave; the gap is uncertain by an order of magnitude and no observable topological signature has been identified.
sources: Dean & Hjorth-Jensen (2003). "Pairing in nuclear systems: from neutron stars to finite nuclei". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 607. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.607](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.607)

name: Positron annihilation maps Fermi surfaces and vacancies
summary: Positrons from beta-plus sources (22Na) thermalize in solids and annihilate with electrons; the angular correlation and Doppler broadening of the 511 keV gammas map the electron momentum density (Fermi surfaces), and positron lifetimes identify vacancies.
map: \rho(\mathbf p)=\sum_j\left|\int e^{-i\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf r}\psi_+(\mathbf r)\psi_j(\mathbf r)\,d\mathbf r\right|^2;\ \Delta\theta\approx p_\perp/m_ec
breaks: The positron wavefunction and electron-positron correlations weight the signal non-uniformly, so momentum densities need theory corrections.
sources: Tuomisto & Makkonen (2013). "Defect identification in semiconductors with positron annihilation: Experiment and theory". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 85, 1583. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.85.1583](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.85.1583)

name: Cryogenic phonon calorimeters for double-beta and endpoints
summary: 0vbb searches (CUORE TeO2 crystals) and electron-capture endpoint measurements use millikelvin calorimeters in which the decay energy becomes phonons; the T^3 Debye heat capacity makes the temperature rise measurable with thermistors or transition-edge sensors.
breaks: Detector physics adds athermal phonon transport and superconducting-sensor physics beyond equilibrium lattice dynamics.
sources: CUORE Collaboration (2022). "Search for Majorana neutrinos exploiting millikelvin cryogenics with CUORE". *Nature* 604, 53. [arXiv:2104.06906](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.06906)

name: Time-dependent DFT of fission and electron dynamics
summary: Microscopic fission dynamics (scission, fragment excitation, neutron emission) is computed with time-dependent superfluid DFT, the nuclear version of the Runge-Gross TDDFT used for electronic excitations and dynamics in materials.
breaks: Nuclear TDDFT lacks quantum fluctuations of the collective coordinates (no spontaneous tunnelling) and uses fitted functionals; electronic TDDFT has an external field and adiabatic xc approximations.
sources: Runge & Gross (1984). "Density-Functional Theory for Time-Dependent Systems". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 52, 997. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.997](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.997)
Bender, Heenen & Reinhard (2003). "Self-consistent mean-field models for nuclear structure". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 121. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121)

name: Collective tunnelling: fission and Josephson junctions
summary: Spontaneous fission and sub-barrier fusion are tunnelling of a collective coordinate coupled to many intrinsic degrees of freedom, the same dissipative macroscopic-tunnelling problem as the phase of a current-biased Josephson junction (Caldeira-Leggett).
breaks: The nuclear collective inertia M(q) and the barrier come from the same nucleons with level crossings, not an ohmic bath; the coupling is non-Markovian and few-channel.
sources: Caldeira & Leggett (1981). "Influence of Dissipation on Quantum Tunneling in Macroscopic Systems". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 46, 211. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.46.211](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.46.211)
Hagino & Takigawa (2012). "Subbarrier Fusion Reactions and Many-Particle Quantum Tunneling". *Prog. Theor. Phys.* 128, 1061. [arXiv:1210.1840](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.1840)

name: Ion channeling, RBS and crystal-blocking lifetimes
summary: Nuclear backscattering and channeling of MeV ions locate impurities and defects in crystals; conversely, crystal blocking of reaction products measures compound-nucleus and fission lifetimes down to ~1e-18 s from the recoil distance travelled before decay.
breaks: Channeling is classical ion optics in a lattice; it gives timing only when recoil displacements are comparable with the Thomas-Fermi screening length.

name: Neutron scattering as the probe of structure and magnetism
summary: The nuclear neutron-scattering length (Fermi pseudopotential) and the neutron magnetic moment make reactor and spallation neutrons the standard probe of crystal structure, magnetic order and phonon and magnon dispersions; antiferromagnetic order was first seen this way.
breaks: b is an empirical nuclear quantity that varies erratically between isotopes (hence isotopic contrast variation), unlike X-ray form factors that scale with Z.
sources: Shull, Strauser & Wollan (1951). "Neutron Diffraction by Paramagnetic and Antiferromagnetic Substances". *Phys. Rev.* 83, 333. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.83.333](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.83.333)

name: Random-matrix statistics: compound nuclei and chaotic dots
summary: Random-matrix theory was born for neutron resonances (Wigner, Porter-Thomas), and its reaction-theory machinery (Mahaux-Weidenmüller S-matrix, Ericson fluctuations) became the theory of transport through chaotic quantum dots: conductance fluctuations and the Landauer conductance as S-matrix statistics.
map: S=1-2\pi iW^\dagger(E-H+i\pi WW^\dagger)^{-1}W,\ H\in\text{GOE};\ G=\frac{2e^2}{h}\mathrm{Tr}\,t^\dagger t
breaks: Nuclear widths probe energy-averaged cross sections of a self-bound system; dot transport adds magnetic-field symmetry classes (GUE), dephasing and Coulomb blockade.
sources: Porter & Thomas (1956). "Fluctuations of Nuclear Reaction Widths". *Phys. Rev.* 104, 483. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.104.483](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.104.483)
Mitchell, Richter & Weidenmüller (2010). "Random matrices and chaos in nuclear physics: Nuclear reactions". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 82, 2845. [arXiv:1001.2422](https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.2422)
Beenakker (1997). "Random-matrix theory of quantum transport". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 69, 731. [arXiv:cond-mat/9612179](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9612179)

name: Thorium-229 nuclear clock in wide-gap crystals
summary: The 8.4 eV isomer of 229Th has been laser-excited in a CaF2 host: the crystal needs a band gap above the transition to suppress internal conversion, and crystal-field and electric-field-gradient effects split and shift the nuclear line.
breaks: The crystal is an environment, not part of the transition; defects, radiation damage and temperature-dependent shifts limit clock performance.
sources: Tiedau et al. (2024). "Laser Excitation of the Th-229 Nucleus". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 132, 182501. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.182501](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.132.182501)

name: Mössbauer effect: recoil-free gamma emission from a lattice
summary: Nuclear gamma rays are emitted and absorbed without recoil because the whole lattice takes the momentum; the recoil-free fraction is the phonon Debye-Waller factor, and Mössbauer spectroscopy reads hyperfine fields, isomer shifts and phonon densities of states in solids.
breaks: Only low-energy, long-lived gamma transitions (57Fe at 14.4 keV) work, and the nuclear linewidth, not phonon physics, sets the resolution.
sources: Mössbauer (1958). "Kernresonanzfluoreszenz von Gammastrahlung in Ir191". *Z. Phys.* 151, 124. [doi:10.1007/BF01344210](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01344210)

name: Homogeneous-matter QMC as functional input
summary: Electronic DFT rests on the QMC energy of the uniform electron gas (LDA); nuclear functionals are anchored the same way to ab initio neutron-matter equations of state, which fix the isovector part of Skyrme EDFs and their neutron-skin and radius predictions.
map: E_{xc}^{\rm LDA}=\int n\,\epsilon_{xc}^{\rm HEG}(n)\,d^3r\ \leftrightarrow\ E_{\rm EDF}\ \text{fitted to}\ E_{\rm PNM}(n)/N
breaks: The electron gas is Coulombic and the LDA is a controlled local limit; neutron matter has spin-isospin-dependent and three-body forces with theory uncertainties, and the map to finite nuclei is a fit, not an exact limit.
sources: Ceperley & Alder (1980). "Ground State of the Electron Gas by a Stochastic Method". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 45, 566. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.566](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.45.566)
Brown (2000). "Neutron Radii in Nuclei and the Neutron Equation of State". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 85, 5296. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.5296](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.5296)
Carlson et al. (2015). "Quantum Monte Carlo methods for nuclear physics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 87, 1067. [arXiv:1412.3081](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3081)

name: SRG/IMSRG and Wegner flow equations
summary: The similarity renormalization group that softens nuclear forces and the in-medium SRG that decouples nuclear ground states are the continuous unitary flow equations introduced by Wegner and by Glazek and Wilson, which are also used for impurity and lattice models in condensed matter.
breaks: Nuclear SRG must track the induced three- and higher-body forces of a vacuum interaction; CM flows usually start from a fixed lattice Hamiltonian and track induced couplings differently.
sources: Wegner (1994). "Flow-equations for Hamiltonians". *Ann. Phys. (Leipzig)* 506, 77. [doi:10.1002/andp.19945060203](https://doi.org/10.1002/andp.19945060203)
Bogner, Furnstahl & Perry (2007). "Similarity renormalization group for nucleon-nucleon interactions". *Phys. Rev. C* 75, 061001. [arXiv:nucl-th/0611045](https://arxiv.org/abs/nucl-th/0611045)
Hergert et al. (2016). "The In-Medium Similarity Renormalization Group: A novel ab initio method for nuclei". *Phys. Rep.* 621, 165. [arXiv:1512.06956](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.06956)

name: Shared quantum Monte Carlo toolkit and sign problem
summary: GFMC/AFDMC and nuclear lattice EFT (auxiliary-field Monte Carlo after a Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation) are the projector and determinant QMC used for Hubbard models; approximate SU(4) Wigner symmetry suppresses the nuclear sign problem as particle-hole symmetry does at half filling, and neural-network states now enter both.
map: e^{-\tau\frac C2\rho^2}\propto\int ds\,e^{-\frac{s^2}{2C\tau}}e^{-\tau s\rho}\ \Rightarrow\ Z=\int\mathcal Ds\,\det M[s]
breaks: Nuclear Hamiltonians have strong spin-isospin and three-body operators that cannot be written as one-body densities, which forces constrained-path approximations; CM lattice models have a simple on-site U.
sources: Carlson et al. (2015). "Quantum Monte Carlo methods for nuclear physics". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 87, 1067. [arXiv:1412.3081](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.3081)
Lee (2009). "Lattice simulations for few- and many-body systems". *Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys.* 63, 117. [arXiv:0804.3501](https://arxiv.org/abs/0804.3501)
Carleo & Troyer (2017). "Solving the quantum many-body problem with artificial neural networks". *Science* 355, 602. [arXiv:1606.02318](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02318)

name: Nuclear energy density functionals as Kohn-Sham DFT
summary: Skyrme, Gogny and relativistic mean-field calculations are self-consistent Kohn-Sham-like schemes: nucleon orbitals in a potential that is the functional derivative of an energy density functional fitted to data, extended to pairing through HFB (compare DFT for superconductors).
map: h=\frac{\delta E[\rho,\tau,\mathbf J,\tilde\rho]}{\delta\rho},\ h\phi_i=\varepsilon_i\phi_i\ \leftrightarrow\ v_{\rm xc}=\frac{\delta E_{\rm xc}[n]}{\delta n}
breaks: Nuclei are self-bound with no external potential, so Hohenberg-Kohn applies only to intrinsic densities; nuclear EDFs break and then restore symmetries and are fitted phenomenologically rather than derived from a known exact functional.
sources: Bender, Heenen & Reinhard (2003). "Self-consistent mean-field models for nuclear structure". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 121. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121)
Kohn & Sham (1965). "Self-Consistent Equations Including Exchange and Correlation Effects". *Phys. Rev.* 140, A1133. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.140.A1133](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.140.A1133)
Vautherin & Brink (1972). "Hartree-Fock Calculations with Skyrme's Interaction. I. Spherical Nuclei". *Phys. Rev. C* 5, 626. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevC.5.626](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.5.626)

name: Particle-vibration coupling vs electron-phonon coupling
summary: Bohr-Mottelson nuclear field theory couples single nucleons to quantized surface 'phonons' just as electrons couple to lattice phonons; the coupling dresses quasiparticles, fragments strength and adds an induced pairing interaction akin to phonon-mediated BCS glue.
map: H_{pv}=\sum_{\lambda\mu}\kappa_\lambda k(r)Y^*_{\lambda\mu}(\hat r)(b^\dagger_{\lambda\mu}+b_{\lambda\mu})\leftrightarrow\sum g_{\mathbf q}(b^\dagger_{\mathbf q}+b_{-\mathbf q})c^\dagger c
breaks: Nuclear phonons are a few discrete collective modes of the same nucleons: no separate lattice, no Debye cutoff and no Migdal small parameter omega/E_F.
sources: Bohr, Mottelson & Pines (1958). "Possible Analogy between the Excitation Spectra of Nuclei and Those of the Superconducting Metallic State". *Phys. Rev.* 110, 936. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.110.936](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.110.936)

name: Giant dipole resonance and cluster surface plasmon
summary: The nuclear giant dipole resonance (protons oscillating against neutrons) and the Mie surface plasmon of metal clusters are both collective dipole modes that exhaust the Thomas-Reiche-Kuhn sum rule, treated with the same RPA and Goldhaber-Teller/Steinwedel-Jensen pictures.
breaks: The GDR restoring force is the isovector symmetry energy, the plasmon's is Coulomb; Landau damping and escape widths differ in size and origin.
sources: Goldhaber & Teller (1948). "On Nuclear Dipole Vibrations". *Phys. Rev.* 74, 1046. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.74.1046](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.74.1046)

Brack (1993). "The physics of simple metal clusters: self-consistent jellium model and semiclassical approaches". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 65, 677. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.65.677](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.65.677)

name: Pairing in finite Fermi systems: nuclei and nanograins
summary: Nuclei and nanometre Al grains are both mesoscopic superconductors whose level spacing is comparable to the gap; the exactly solvable Richardson pairing model describes both, and the nuclear odd-even mass effect is the parity effect seen in grain spectroscopy and superconducting single-electron transistors.
breaks: Grains have a Coulomb charging energy and an electron bath; nuclei have two particle species, deformation and spin-orbit-split shells, so level statistics and blocking differ.
sources: Richardson (1963). "A restricted class of exact eigenstates of the pairing-force Hamiltonian". *Phys. Lett.* 3, 277. [doi:10.1016/0031-9163(63)90259-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/0031-9163(63)90259-2)

Dukelsky, Pittel & Sierra (2004). "Colloquium: Exactly solvable Richardson-Gaudin models for many-body quantum systems". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 76, 643. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.76.643](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.76.643)

Black, Ralph & Tinkham (1996). "Spectroscopy of the Superconducting Gap in Individual Nanometer-Scale Aluminum Particles". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 76, 688. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.688](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.76.688)

name: Shell structure and magic numbers in clusters and dots
summary: Alkali-metal clusters show magic numbers 8, 20, 40, 58 and quantum dots show shell filling with Hund's rule; both are understood with nuclear tools (mean-field shells, Strutinsky shell corrections, Nilsson-type deformation). Quantum dots are 'artificial atoms' and clusters 'electronic nuclei'.
map: E=E_{\rm LD}+\delta E_{\rm shell},\ \delta E=\sum_i\epsilon_i-\tilde E;\ \text{2D HO dot: }2,6,12,20\ \leftrightarrow\ \text{3D HO: }2,8,20,40
breaks: Electron systems lack spin-orbit-driven magic numbers (no 28, 50, 82) and are Coulomb-repulsive and externally confined; nuclei are self-bound with short-range forces.
sources: Knight et al. (1984). "Electronic Shell Structure and Abundances of Sodium Clusters". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 52, 2141. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.2141](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.52.2141)
Tarucha et al. (1996). "Shell Filling and Spin Effects in a Few Electron Quantum Dot". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 77, 3613. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.3613](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.77.3613)
Strutinsky (1967). "Shell effects in nuclear masses and deformation energies". *Nucl. Phys. A* 95, 420. [doi:10.1016/0375-9474(67)90510-6](https://doi.org/10.1016/0375-9474(67)90510-6)

name: Landau Fermi-liquid theory of nuclei and nuclear matter
summary: Independent-particle shells survive a strong NN force because the relevant objects are Landau quasiparticles near the Fermi surface; Migdal's theory of finite Fermi systems uses Landau parameters (effective mass, spin-isospin g') as electron Fermi-liquid theory does, and giant resonances are its zero-sound-like modes.
breaks: Nuclei are finite and self-bound with two species and a strong tensor force; quasiparticle lifetimes are short away from the Fermi surface and strength fragmentation is large.
sources: Shankar (1994). "Renormalization-group approach to interacting fermions". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 66, 129. [arXiv:cond-mat/9307009](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9307009)
Bender, Heenen & Reinhard (2003). "Self-consistent mean-field models for nuclear structure". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 121. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.121)

name: Shape phase transitions as finite-size quantum criticality
summary: Along isotopic chains nuclei change from spherical to deformed as the control parameter N varies; Landau theory in quadrupole collective coordinates and the critical-point symmetries E(5)/X(5) treat this as a quantum phase transition with finite-N precursors.
breaks: Nuclei never reach a thermodynamic limit, N is discrete, and there is no spatial correlation length, quantum critical fan or non-Fermi-liquid transport.
sources: Cejnar, Jolie & Casten (2010). "Quantum phase transitions in the shapes of atomic nuclei". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 82, 2155. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.82.2155](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.82.2155)

Iachello (2001). "Analytic Description of Critical-Point Nuclei in a Spherical-Axially Deformed Shape Phase Transition". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 87, 052502. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.052502](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.052502)

name: Nuclear pairing is BCS pairing
summary: Odd-even mass staggering, the gap in even-even spectra and reduced moments of inertia follow from the BCS gap equation with a short-range NN attraction near the nuclear Fermi surface; Bohr, Mottelson and Pines carried BCS over to nuclei within a year.
breaks: Nuclei hold only ~10 pairs, so BCS particle-number fluctuations matter (projection needed) and the coherence length exceeds the nucleus; the pairing glue is the bare nuclear force, not a retarded phonon.
sources: Bohr, Mottelson & Pines (1958). "Possible Analogy between the Excitation Spectra of Nuclei and Those of the Superconducting Metallic State". *Phys. Rev.* 110, 936. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.110.936](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.110.936)
Bardeen, Cooper & Schrieffer (1957). "Theory of Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 108, 1175. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.108.1175)
Dean & Hjorth-Jensen (2003). "Pairing in nuclear systems: from neutron stars to finite nuclei". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 75, 607. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.75.607](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.75.607)

name: Rotation vs magnetic field: backbending and Meissner
summary: The Coriolis force on a rotating nucleus acts on time-reversed pairs as a magnetic field acts on Cooper pairs; pairing quenches the moment of inertia below the rigid value (like Meissner screening), and backbending at high spin is the analogue of the critical field that destroys superconductivity.
map: H'=H-\omega J_x\leftrightarrow H-\mu_B\mathbf B\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma;\ \mathcal I<\mathcal I_{\rm rigid}\leftrightarrow\chi<0;\ \omega_c\leftrightarrow H_c
breaks: The cranking 'field' couples to the orbital angular momentum of a finite drop, not to a gauge field; there is no flux expulsion, London length or vortex phase, and the transition is smeared by finite size.
sources: Mottelson & Valatin (1960). "Effect of Nuclear Rotation on the Pairing Correlation". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 5, 511. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.5.511](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.5.511)
Migdal (1959). "Superfluidity and the moments of inertia of nuclei". *Nucl. Phys.* 13, 655. [doi:10.1016/0029-5582(59)90264-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/0029-5582(59)90264-0)

name: Itinerant versus local-moment magnetism
summary: Stoner ferromagnetism and spin-density waves arise from band structure and Fermi surface nesting, contrasting with Heisenberg local moments; RKKY links conduction electrons to local moments.

name: Bloch bands to Berry curvature and Chern numbers
summary: Berry connection defined on Bloch eigenstates over the Brillouin zone gives Chern and Z2 invariants; band theory supplies the Hilbert-space bundle that topology classifies.

name: DFT as input to DMFT and QMC
summary: Kohn–Sham band structures supply downfolded tight-binding models for DMFT (DFT+DMFT), and QMC benchmarks exchange–correlation functionals; both address the many-electron problem at different accuracy and cost.

name: DFT prediction of hydride superconductors
summary: DFT structure search plus linear-response phonons and Eliashberg theory predicted H3S and LaH10 Tc before experiment, a rare first-principles prediction of Tc.

name: Coulomb blockade and Landauer transport in dots
summary: Quantum-dot conductance is analysed with Landauer–Büttiker and master-equation transport; conductance quantization and resonant tunnelling in mesoscopic wires carry over to dots.

name: Landauer–Büttiker edge channels
summary: Landauer–Büttiker formalism with chiral edge channels explains quantized Hall resistance, and quantized conductance in mesoscopic wires shares the same transmission-mode counting.

name: Phonon-mediated pairing
summary: Electron–phonon coupling gives the retarded attraction behind Cooper pairing; the isotope effect and Debye frequency set Tc prefactors in BCS and Eliashberg theory.

name: High-frequency hydrogen phonons drive high Tc
summary: Light hydrogen gives very high phonon frequencies and strong electron–phonon coupling, so BCS/Eliashberg Tc scales with the phonon energy scale.

name: Semiconductor physics in monolayer TMDs
summary: TMD monolayers are direct-gap 2D semiconductors where doping, heterojunctions and carrier statistics carry over, but reduced screening gives huge exciton binding energies beyond the 3D Wannier picture.

name: Wannier excitons in semiconductors vs TMDs
summary: Excitons are hydrogen-like electron–hole bound states in both; TMD monolayers have nonlocal screening that modifies the Rydberg series.
breaks: In 2D the dielectric screening is nonlocal (Keldysh), so the hydrogenic series fails for excited states.

name: 2D materials as topological platforms
summary: Graphene, TMDs and moiré systems host Dirac cones, Chern bands, quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall states, linking low-dimensional materials to topological classification.

name: Relativistic quantum Hall effect in graphene
summary: Dirac electrons in graphene give half-integer quantum Hall plateaus from the zero-energy n=0 Landau level and Berry phase pi.

name: Graphene as a 2D Dirac semimetal
summary: Graphene's Dirac points are the 2D counterpart of 3D Weyl/Dirac nodes; both are linear band crossings with Berry phase and relativistic-like quasiparticles.
breaks: Graphene nodes need C2T and are not topologically protected against gap opening by symmetry-breaking substrates; 3D Weyl nodes are stable monopoles of Berry flux.

name: Weyl/Dirac nodes and graphene Dirac cones
summary: Weyl and Dirac semimetals generalise graphene's Dirac cones to 3D, with Fermi arcs and chiral anomaly replacing edge zero modes and half-integer Hall response.
breaks: Graphene has no Fermi arcs or net chirality per valley pair in the same sense and the nodes are not monopoles.

name: Fractional Chern insulators in moiré bands
summary: Flat Chern bands in twisted MoTe2 and graphene host fractional Chern insulators at zero field, lattice analogues of fractional quantum Hall states with anyonic excitations.

name: Moiré superlattices as tunable Hubbard simulators
summary: Twisted TMD bilayers realise triangular-lattice Hubbard models with tunable U/W, showing Mott insulators and superconductivity-like phases; magic-angle graphene correlated insulators arise from flat-band Coulomb repulsion.

name: Hofstadter bands and Chern bands in moiré systems
summary: Moiré superlattices produce Hofstadter butterflies at accessible fields and Chern bands with quantized Hall response at zero field, linking Landau levels to flat Chern bands and Wannier diagrams.

name: Kondo effect in quantum dots
summary: A dot with an odd electron number acts as a tunable Anderson impurity, producing a Kondo resonance and unitary conductance at low T that realises single-impurity Kondo physics in a controlled device.

name: Majorana nanowires and dot arrays
summary: Semiconductor nanowires with spin–orbit coupling, Zeeman field and proximity superconductivity realise Kitaev-chain physics; quantum dot chains build minimal Kitaev chains and probe zero-bias peaks.

name: Valleytronics and spin-valley locking vs spintronics
summary: Spin–valley locking in TMDs lets valley act as a degree of freedom, analogous to spin; valley Hall effect parallels spin Hall effect via Berry curvature, and magnons and excitons share bosonic transport ideas.
breaks: Valley is not a conserved quantum number against intervalley scattering and lacks a simple torque or conservation law like spin transfer.

name: Altermagnets: spin splitting and anomalous Hall
summary: Symmetry-enforced spin-split bands in altermagnets generate anomalous Hall responses via Berry curvature despite zero net magnetization, connecting magnetic point-group symmetry to band geometry.

name: Superexchange from the Hubbard model
summary: At half filling and large U the Hubbard model reduces to the Heisenberg antiferromagnet by second-order virtual hopping, deriving Anderson superexchange.

name: Spin glasses and structural glasses
summary: Frustration and rugged energy landscapes link spin glasses to structural glasses; replica symmetry breaking and random first-order transition theory connect the two.
breaks: Not stated by the analyst.

name: Order-by-disorder and defect physics across spin and nematic systems
summary: Both study order-parameter manifolds with topological defects (vortices, hedgehogs, disclinations) classified by homotopy; spin ice and nematics share Coulomb-gas-like defect interactions and degenerate manifolds.
breaks: Spin liquids are quantum with fractionalized excitations and entanglement, while nematics are classical thermal systems with Frank elasticity.

name: Quantum spin liquids as topologically ordered states
summary: Gapped spin liquids host fractionalised spinons and visons with topological ground-state degeneracy; the Kitaev honeycomb model realises Z2 gauge theory with Majorana excitations.

name: Skyrmion topological Hall effect and emergent fields
summary: Electrons traversing a skyrmion texture acquire a real-space Berry phase, producing an emergent magnetic field and topological Hall effect, the real-space counterpart of momentum-space Berry curvature.

name: Active nematics
summary: Active nematics combine Frank elasticity and defect dynamics of liquid crystals with active stress, producing spontaneous flows and self-propelled +1/2 disclinations.

name: FQHE as prototype topological order
summary: The fractional quantum Hall effect, with Laughlin quasiparticles of fractional charge and statistics, is the archetype of topological order, with chiral edge modes and ground-state degeneracy on a torus.

name: Majorana zero modes as non-Abelian anyons
summary: Vortex Majorana modes in p+ip superconductors obey Ising non-Abelian statistics, the basis of topological quantum computation and the Moore–Read fractional quantum Hall analogy.

name: Heavy-fermion quantum critical points
summary: Heavy-fermion metals such as CeCu6-xAux are canonical quantum critical systems, where Kondo breakdown competes with RKKY magnetism in a Doniach phase diagram and yields non-Fermi-liquid behaviour.

name: Numerical solutions of the Hubbard model
summary: DMFT, DQMC, DMRG and tensor networks were developed and benchmarked on the Hubbard model; DMFT captures the Mott transition as a mean-field in infinite dimensions.

name: Doped Mott insulator and cuprate superconductivity
summary: Cuprates are doped Mott insulators described by the Hubbard/t-J model; d-wave pairing emerges from superexchange-driven correlations (RVB).

name: Strange metal normal state of cuprates
summary: Optimally doped cuprates show T-linear resistivity and a possible quantum critical point under the superconducting dome; non-Fermi-liquid scattering near Planckian bound.

name: Unconventional superconductivity near a quantum critical point
summary: Iron pnictides show a superconducting dome around a putative antiferromagnetic quantum critical point with T-linear resistivity, suggesting spin-fluctuation pairing as in cuprates and heavy fermions.

name: BdG quasiparticles and topological superconductivity
summary: Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonians of BCS theory carry particle-hole symmetry; for p-wave or engineered pairing their topology yields Majorana modes, as in the Kitaev chain.

name: Fractional Josephson effect
summary: Topological Josephson junctions host Majorana-mediated 4π-periodic current-phase relations, a signature that differs from the 2π conventional Josephson effect.

name: Band theory of neutrons in the neutron-star crust
summary: Bragg scattering of unbound superfluid neutrons by the nuclear lattice of the inner crust is computed with Bloch's theorem and band-structure methods; the resulting large neutron effective mass (entrainment) reduces the mobile superfluid fraction and challenges crust-only glitch models.
map: \psi_{nk}(\mathbf r+\mathbf R)=e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf R}\psi_{nk}(\mathbf r):\ \text{electrons}\to\text{free neutrons};\ m_n^*/m_n\gg1\ (\text{entrainment})
sources: Chamel (2013). "Crustal Entrainment and Pulsar Glitches". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 110, 011101. [arXiv:1210.8177](https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.8177)
Chamel & Haensel (2008). "Physics of Neutron Star Crusts". *Living Rev. Relativ.* 11, 10. [arXiv:0812.3955](https://arxiv.org/abs/0812.3955)

name: Degenerate Fermi gas: metals and white dwarfs
summary: The same degenerate Fermi-Dirac electron gas gives the Sommerfeld model of metals and the pressure that supports white dwarfs; Fowler applied Fermi statistics to white dwarfs in 1926, before Sommerfeld applied it to metals, and relativistic kinematics turns P~n^{5/3} into P~n^{4/3}, giving the Chandrasekhar mass.
sources: Fowler (1926). "On Dense Matter". *Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc.* 87, 114. [doi:10.1093/mnras/87.2.114](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/87.2.114)
Chandrasekhar (1931). "The Maximum Mass of Ideal White Dwarfs". *Astrophys. J.* 74, 81. [doi:10.1086/143324](https://doi.org/10.1086/143324)

name: Superionic water ice in ice-giant interiors
summary: Superionic water, an oxygen crystal through which protons diffuse like a liquid, was predicted by ab initio simulation for Uranus and Neptune and identified in laser-shock experiments by nanosecond X-ray diffraction (fcc ice XVIII); it may explain the ice giants' non-dipolar magnetic fields.
sources: Cavazzoni et al. (1999). "Superionic and Metallic States of Water and Ammonia at Giant Planet Conditions". *Science* 283, 44. [doi:10.1126/science.283.5398.44](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.283.5398.44)
Millot et al. (2019). "Nanosecond X-ray diffraction of shock-compressed superionic water ice". *Nature* 569, 251. [doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1114-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1114-6)

name: Coulomb crystallization of white-dwarf cores
summary: Carbon-oxygen ions in a cooling white dwarf freeze into a bcc Coulomb (one-component-plasma) crystal near Gamma~175; Gaia's cooling-sequence pile-up confirmed latent-heat release and phase separation, and the same bcc Coulomb lattice makes up neutron-star crusts.
sources: Van Horn (1968). "Crystallization of White Dwarfs". *Astrophys. J.* 151, 227. [doi:10.1086/149432](https://doi.org/10.1086/149432)

Tremblay et al. (2019). "Core crystallization and pile-up in the cooling sequence of evolving white dwarfs". *Nature* 565, 202. [doi:10.1038/s41586-018-0791-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0791-x)

name: DFT and dielectric response for dark-matter scattering
summary: Dark-matter-electron scattering rates in crystals are computed from DFT crystal form factors and, with screening included, from the energy-loss function Im[-1/eps(q,omega)], so electronic-structure codes directly set direct-detection sensitivities.
sources: Essig et al. (2016). "Direct Detection of sub-GeV Dark Matter with Semiconductor Targets". *J. High Energy Phys.* 05, 046. [arXiv:1509.01598](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.01598)
Knapen, Kozaczuk & Lin (2021). "Dark matter-electron scattering in dielectrics". *Phys. Rev. D* 104, 015031. [arXiv:2101.08275](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.08275)

name: Ab initio equations of state for giant-planet interiors
summary: DFT-based molecular dynamics provides the hydrogen-helium equation of state and the H-He immiscibility ('helium rain') used in Jupiter and Saturn interior models fitted to Juno and Cassini gravity data; DFT exchange-correlation and band-gap errors directly shift the predicted metallization boundary.
sources: Morales et al. (2009). "Phase separation in hydrogen-helium mixtures at Mbar pressures". *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci.* 106, 1324. [doi:10.1073/pnas.0812581106](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0812581106)

name: Electron transport in white-dwarf and neutron-star matter
summary: Thermal and electrical conductivities of degenerate stellar matter are computed with the Boltzmann/Ziman theory of metals (electron-phonon Umklapp and electron-impurity scattering, Wiedemann-Franz); crust-cooling curves of accreting neutron stars imply a low-impurity, ordered rather than amorphous crust.
sources: Potekhin et al. (1999). "Transport properties of degenerate electrons in neutron star envelopes and white dwarf cores". *Astron. Astrophys.* 346, 345. [arXiv:astro-ph/9903127](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9903127)
Brown & Cumming (2009). "Mapping Crustal Heating with the Cooling Light Curves of Quasi-Persistent Transients". *Astrophys. J.* 698, 1020. [arXiv:0901.3115](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.3115)

name: Single-phonon excitations for sub-MeV dark matter
summary: Below ~MeV the dark matter's momentum transfer is below the inverse lattice spacing, so it scatters by creating single acoustic or optical phonons rather than nuclear recoils; polar crystals (GaAs, sapphire) with dark-photon-coupled optical phonons are proposed targets read out by phonon sensors.
sources: Knapen et al. (2018). "Detection of Light Dark Matter With Optical Phonons in Polar Materials". *Phys. Lett. B* 785, 386. [arXiv:1712.06598](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.06598)

name: Crustal shear modes as magnetar QPOs
summary: Quasi-periodic oscillations in magnetar giant-flare tails (tens of Hz) are interpreted as global torsional modes of the crystalline crust, i.e. long-wavelength transverse acoustic phonons of the Coulomb lattice whose speed is set by the shear modulus mu~0.12 n_i Z^2 e^2/a.
sources: Strohmayer & Watts (2005). "Discovery of Fast X-Ray Oscillations during the 1998 Giant Flare from SGR 1900+14". *Astrophys. J.* 632, L111. [arXiv:astro-ph/0508206](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0508206)

name: Debye cooling of crystallized white dwarfs
summary: Once a white-dwarf core crystallizes, its ionic heat capacity follows the Debye phonon law and falls as T^3 below Theta_D, so the oldest white dwarfs cool faster ('Debye cooling'), which shapes the faint end of the luminosity function used for cosmochronology.
sources: Tremblay et al. (2019). "Core crystallization and pile-up in the cooling sequence of evolving white dwarfs". *Nature* 565, 202. [doi:10.1038/s41586-018-0791-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0791-x)

name: Semiconductor targets for dark-matter electron recoils
summary: Silicon and germanium crystals are dark-matter targets: ionization-plus-phonon detectors for nuclear recoils, and single-electron skipper CCDs (SENSEI, DAMIC-M) whose ~1 eV band gap lets sub-GeV dark matter register through electron excitations across the gap.
sources: Essig, Mardon & Volansky (2012). "Direct Detection of Sub-GeV Dark Matter". *Phys. Rev. D* 85, 076007. [arXiv:1108.5383](https://arxiv.org/abs/1108.5383)

SENSEI Collaboration (2025). "First Direct-Detection Results on Sub-GeV Dark Matter Using the SENSEI Detector at SNOLAB". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 134, 011804. [arXiv:2312.13342](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.13342)

name: Fullerenes and PAHs: carbon nanostructures in space
summary: C60 was discovered in laser-vaporization experiments built to mimic carbon-star chemistry, opening the fullerene-nanotube-graphene family of carbon materials; fullerenes were later found in planetary nebulae and C60+ identified as a diffuse-interstellar-band carrier.
sources: Kroto et al. (1985). "C60: Buckminsterfullerene". *Nature* 318, 162. [doi:10.1038/318162a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/318162a0)
Cami et al. (2010). "Detection of C60 and C70 in a Young Planetary Nebula". *Science* 329, 1180. [doi:10.1126/science.1192035](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1192035)
Campbell et al. (2015). "Laboratory confirmation of C60+ as the carrier of two diffuse interstellar bands". *Nature* 523, 322. [doi:10.1038/nature14566](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14566)

name: Wigner crystals and stellar Coulomb crystals
summary: Electron Wigner crystals in moire TMD superlattices and the ion crystals of white dwarfs and neutron-star crusts are both one-component plasmas that crystallize in a uniform neutralizing background once Coulomb energy beats kinetic energy (large r_s or large Gamma).
breaks: Stellar ions melt classically through thermal fluctuations, while 2D electron Wigner crystals melt quantum mechanically; moire Wigner crystals are pinned to an imposed superlattice and are two-dimensional.
sources: Regan et al. (2020). "Mott and generalized Wigner crystal states in WSe2/WS2 moiré superlattices". *Nature* 579, 359. [arXiv:1910.09047](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.09047)

name: Emergent monopoles in spin ice and the monopole problem
summary: Spin-ice excitations behave as deconfined magnetic monopoles with a Coulomb interaction, a condensed-matter realization of the monopoles whose predicted overproduction at grand-unified transitions motivated inflation.
breaks: Spin-ice monopoles source the H field (div M), not B; they are emergent quasiparticles with non-quantized, material-set charge, unlike 't Hooft-Polyakov monopoles of a broken gauge group.
sources: Castelnovo, Moessner & Sondhi (2008). "Magnetic monopoles in spin ice". *Nature* 451, 42. [arXiv:0710.5515](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.5515)

name: Skyrmions and cosmic textures
summary: Magnetic skyrmions and cosmological textures are both non-singular topological solitons of a sphere-valued order parameter classified by homotopy (pi_2 for 2D films, pi_3 for 3D cosmic textures); a collapsing texture was proposed to explain the CMB Cold Spot.
breaks: Skyrmions are static, DMI-stabilized and 2D; cosmic textures are 3D, unstable to collapse by Derrick's theorem and scale with the horizon. The Cold Spot texture interpretation is not established.
sources: Turok (1989). "Global texture as the origin of cosmic structure". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 63, 2625. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.2625](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.2625)
Cruz et al. (2007). "A Cosmic Microwave Background Feature Consistent with a Cosmic Texture". *Science* 318, 1612. [arXiv:0710.5737](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.5737)

name: Dust aggregation: from colloids to planetesimals
summary: The first stage of planet formation is aggregation of micron dust grains by Brownian motion and differential drift into fractal aggregates, followed by compaction, bouncing and fragmentation: the cluster-cluster aggregation and contact mechanics studied in colloids and granular matter.
map: D=\frac{k_BT}{6\pi\eta a}\to t_s=\frac{\rho_sa}{\rho_gv_{th}}\ (\text{Epstein});\ N\propto R^{d_f},\ d_f\approx1.8\text{-}2
sources: Blum & Wurm (2008). "The Growth Mechanisms of Macroscopic Bodies in Protoplanetary Disks". *Annu. Rev. Astron. Astrophys.* 46, 21. [doi:10.1146/annurev.astro.46.060407.145152](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.astro.46.060407.145152)

name: Rubble-pile asteroids as granular bodies
summary: Most km-sized asteroids (Itokawa, Ryugu, Bennu) are gravitationally bound granular aggregates whose shapes, spin limits, regolith segregation and response to spacecraft contact are governed by granular rheology, friction and weak cohesion.
sources: Walsh (2018). "Rubble Pile Asteroids". *Annu. Rev. Astron. Astrophys.* 56, 593. [doi:10.1146/annurev-astro-081817-052013](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-astro-081817-052013)

name: Amorphous ices and silicates in disks and dust
summary: Interstellar and protoplanetary grains are largely amorphous: vapour-deposited amorphous solid water and glassy silicates whose crystallization (annealing near the star) and glass-transition kinetics record thermal history and control volatile trapping at snow lines.

name: Kibble-Zurek defects: liquid crystals and the early universe
summary: Kibble's argument that causally disconnected regions choose independent vacua at a symmetry-breaking transition, leaving strings and monopoles whose overabundance inflation must dilute, was tested by quenching nematic liquid crystals and counting disclinations; Zurek's refinement gives defect density from the quench rate.
breaks: Nematic defects form in a dissipative, non-relativistic fluid with no gauge field and coarsen by friction; cosmic defects are relativistic, may be gauge strings, and evolve in an expanding spacetime.
sources: Kibble (1976). "Topology of cosmic domains and strings". *J. Phys. A* 9, 1387. [doi:10.1088/0305-4470/9/8/029](https://doi.org/10.1088/0305-4470/9/8/029)
Zurek (1985). "Cosmological experiments in superfluid helium?". *Nature* 317, 505. [doi:10.1038/317505a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/317505a0)
Chuang et al. (1991). "Cosmology in the Laboratory: Defect Dynamics in Liquid Crystals". *Science* 251, 1336. [doi:10.1126/science.251.4999.1336](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.251.4999.1336)

name: Nuclear pasta as a liquid crystal
summary: In the neutron-star mantle, competition between nuclear surface tension and long-range Coulomb repulsion produces rod, slab and bubble 'pasta' phases with the symmetries of columnar and smectic liquid crystals (and of block-copolymer microphases); their elasticity is described with liquid-crystal theory.
breaks: Pasta is ordered by nuclear plus Coulomb forces at ~1e14 g/cm^3 with no solvent or thermal softness; its elastic constants are MeV-scale and the phases sit in a degenerate electron sea.
sources: Pethick & Potekhin (1998). "Liquid crystals in the mantles of neutron stars". *Phys. Lett. B* 427, 7. [arXiv:astro-ph/9803154](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9803154)
Caplan & Horowitz (2017). "Colloquium: Astromaterial science and nuclear pasta". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 89, 041002. [arXiv:1606.03646](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.03646)

name: Superconducting detectors for the CMB: TES and MKIDs
summary: CMB experiments (BICEP/Keck, SPT, ACT, Simons Observatory, CMB-S4) use arrays of transition-edge-sensor bolometers biased on the steep R(T) of a superconducting transition, and kinetic-inductance detectors that sense photon pair breaking through the Cooper-pair kinetic inductance.
sources: Irwin (1995). "An application of electrothermal feedback for high resolution cryogenic particle detection". *Appl. Phys. Lett.* 66, 1998. [doi:10.1063/1.113674](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.113674)
Day et al. (2003). "A broadband superconducting detector suitable for use in large arrays". *Nature* 425, 817. [doi:10.1038/nature02037](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02037)

name: Cosmic-string formation simulated in superfluid 3He
summary: Neutron-absorption hot spots in BCS-paired superfluid 3He re-cool through Tc and nucleate vortex tangles at the rate predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, a laboratory test of defect formation in early-universe phase transitions with a multicomponent order parameter.
breaks: 3He is a non-relativistic p-wave condensate whose vortices are global (no gauge field), whereas GUT strings are relativistic and typically local; the quench is spatially inhomogeneous, unlike a cosmological transition.
sources: Bäuerle et al. (1996). "Laboratory simulation of cosmic string formation in the early Universe using superfluid 3He". *Nature* 382, 332. [doi:10.1038/382332a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/382332a0)
Ruutu et al. (1996). "Vortex formation in neutron-irradiated superfluid 3He as an analogue of cosmic-string formation". *Nature* 382, 334. [doi:10.1038/382334a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/382334a0)

name: Superconducting phonon sensors and targets for dark matter
summary: Cryogenic dark-matter searches (SuperCDMS, CRESST) read athermal phonons from keV nuclear recoils with tungsten transition-edge sensors; superconductors themselves are proposed as targets for keV-mass dark matter because the gap 2Delta~meV sets an ultra-low threshold.
sources: Hochberg, Zhao & Zurek (2016). "Superconducting Detectors for Superlight Dark Matter". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 116, 011301. [arXiv:1504.07237](https://arxiv.org/abs/1504.07237)

name: Cosmic rays and pair breaking in superconducting devices
summary: Cosmic-ray muons and environmental gamma rays deposit energy in substrates as athermal phonons that break Cooper pairs, causing correlated quasiparticle bursts and error avalanches in superconducting qubits; this is the pair-breaking channel that cryogenic detectors use to see particles.
sources: McEwen et al. (2022). "Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits". *Nat. Phys.* 18, 107. [arXiv:2104.05219](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.05219)
Vepsäläinen et al. (2020). "Impact of ionizing radiation on superconducting qubit coherence". *Nature* 584, 551. [arXiv:2001.09190](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.09190)

name: Nucleon pairing and neutron-star superfluidity
summary: The BCS gap equation with nuclear instead of phonon attraction gives 1S0 neutron superfluidity in the inner crust and 3P2 neutron and 1S0 proton pairing in the core; pair-breaking-formation neutrino emission just below Tc explains the rapid cooling of the Cas A neutron star.
sources: Baym, Pethick & Pines (1969). "Superfluidity in Neutron Stars". *Nature* 224, 673. [doi:10.1038/224673a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/224673a0)

Page et al. (2011). "Rapid Cooling of the Neutron Star in Cassiopeia A Triggered by Neutron Superfluidity in Dense Matter". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 106, 081101. [arXiv:1011.6142](https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.6142)

name: Vortex pinning and creep: flux lines vs pulsar glitches
summary: Pulsar glitches are modelled as catastrophic unpinning of quantized neutron-superfluid vortices from the crust lattice, the physics of Abrikosov flux-line pinning and Anderson-Kim thermally activated flux creep in type-II superconductors; post-glitch relaxation is vortex creep.
map: \oint\mathbf v_s\cdot d\mathbf l=h/2m_n\ (\text{neutron vortex})\leftrightarrow\Phi_0=h/2e\ (\text{flux line});\ \text{Magnus}\leftrightarrow\text{Lorentz force}
breaks: Neutron vortices are neutral and feel Magnus rather than Lorentz forces; pinning sites are nuclei of a Coulomb lattice, not material defects, and entrainment couples the superfluid to the crust.
sources: Anderson & Itoh (1975). "Pulsar glitches and restlessness as a hard superfluidity phenomenon". *Nature* 256, 25. [doi:10.1038/256025a0](https://doi.org/10.1038/256025a0)
Andersson et al. (2012). "Pulsar Glitches: The Crust is not Enough". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 109, 241103. [arXiv:1207.0633](https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.0633)

name: Metallic hydrogen in giant planets
summary: Metallic hydrogen, predicted by Wigner and Huntington and proposed by Ashcroft as a high-Tc phonon superconductor (the idea behind hydride superconductors), makes up most of Jupiter's and Saturn's interiors, where its conductivity powers their dynamos; shock and static compression of the insulator-metal transition serve both fields.
sources: Wigner & Huntington (1935). "On the Possibility of a Metallic Modification of Hydrogen". *J. Chem. Phys.* 3, 764. [doi:10.1063/1.1749590](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1749590)
Ashcroft (1968). "Metallic Hydrogen: A High-Temperature Superconductor?". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 21, 1748. [doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.21.1748](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.21.1748)
Celliers et al. (2018). "Insulator-metal transition in dense fluid deuterium". *Science* 361, 677. [doi:10.1126/science.aat0970](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aat0970)

name: SQUID multiplexed readout of detector arrays
summary: Kilo- to hundred-thousand-pixel TES arrays for CMB polarimetry are read out with SQUID amplifiers in time-division or microwave (rf-SQUID resonator) multiplexing, exploiting the flux-periodic Josephson response and its low noise.

name: Josephson parametric amplifiers in axion haloscopes
summary: Axion haloscopes (ADMX, HAYSTAC) detect axion-to-photon conversion in a microwave cavity with Josephson parametric amplifiers operating near the standard quantum limit, and HAYSTAC's squeezed-vacuum readout beats it.
sources: Du et al. (2018). "Search for Invisible Axion Dark Matter with the Axion Dark Matter Experiment". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 120, 151301. [arXiv:1804.05750](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.05750)
Backes et al. (2021). "A quantum enhanced search for dark matter axions". *Nature* 590, 238. [arXiv:2008.01853](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.01853)

name: Axion quasiparticles in magnetic topological insulators
summary: Magnetic topological insulators host a dynamical axion field theta(t) coupling as theta E.B; its quasiparticle (a longitudinal antiferromagnetic magnon mode) is proposed as a tunable meV-scale medium that converts axion dark matter into THz photons.
map: \mathcal L_\theta=\frac{\theta e^2}{2\pi h}\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B\leftrightarrow\mathcal L_a=g_{a\gamma\gamma}\,a\,\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf B
breaks: The solid-state axion is an emergent collective mode with a material-set mass, not the QCD axion; only the electrodynamic coupling form is shared, and no candidate material is yet confirmed.
sources: Marsh et al. (2019). "Proposal to Detect Dark Matter using Axionic Topological Antiferromagnets". *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 123, 121601. [arXiv:1807.08810](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.08810)

name: Dirac materials as light dark-matter targets
summary: 3D Dirac and Weyl semimetals with meV-scale gaps and weak in-medium screening have been proposed as targets for sub-MeV dark matter scattering or absorption on electrons, with directional sensitivity from anisotropic Dirac cones.
map: H_W=\hbar v_F\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf k,\ E_g\to\text{meV};\ v_F\ll c\ \text{matches DM kinematics}
sources: Hochberg et al. (2018). "Detection of sub-MeV dark matter with three-dimensional Dirac materials". *Phys. Rev. D* 97, 015004. [arXiv:1708.08929](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.08929)

name: X-ray diffraction and Thomson scattering of shocked matter
summary: Crystallography and inelastic scattering move into high-energy-density physics: nanosecond X-ray diffraction identifies crystal structures in laser-shocked samples, and X-ray Thomson scattering measures the dynamic structure factor S(k,omega), the same quantity inelastic X-ray and neutron scattering measure in solids, to infer temperature and ionization.
map: \frac{d^2\sigma}{d\Omega d\omega}=\sigma_T\frac{k_1}{k_0}S(\mathbf k,\omega),\ \mathbf k=\mathbf k_1-\mathbf k_0\ (\text{Bragg: }\mathbf k=\mathbf G)
sources: Glenzer & Redmer (2009). "X-ray Thomson scattering in high energy density plasmas". *Rev. Mod. Phys.* 81, 1625. [doi:10.1103/RevModPhys.81.1625](https://doi.org/10.1103/RevModPhys.81.1625)
Millot et al. (2019). "Nanosecond X-ray diffraction of shock-compressed superionic water ice". *Nature* 569, 251. [doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1114-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1114-6)

name: Neutron damage and defects in fusion materials
summary: 14 MeV fusion neutrons create displacement cascades (vacancies, interstitials, transmutation helium) in tungsten and steel walls; point-defect and dislocation physics of crystals, measured in dpa, sets component lifetime.

name: DFT molecular dynamics for warm dense matter
summary: Equations of state, conductivities and opacities of warm dense matter (solid density, eV temperatures, partially degenerate) are computed with finite-temperature Kohn-Sham DFT molecular dynamics borrowed from electronic-structure theory, with Mermin's finite-T functional and temperature-dependent exchange-correlation.

name: Boltzmann transport in solids and plasma kinetics
summary: Semiclassical electron transport in crystals solves the same kinetic equation as plasma physics, with a Lorentz-force streaming term and a collision integral (relaxation-time or Fokker-Planck); Landau damping of plasmons into the electron-hole continuum is the solid-state counterpart of collisionless Landau damping.
map:
\partial_tf+\mathbf v\cdot
abla_{\mathbf r}f+ rac{q}{\hbar}(\mathbf E+\mathbf v	imes\mathbf B)\cdot
abla_{\mathbf k}f=C[f],\ \mathbf v=\hbar^{-1}
abla_{\mathbf k}\epsilon_n(\mathbf k)
breaks: Solid-state carriers have band dispersions and Fermi-Dirac statistics with Pauli-blocked collisions and Umklapp; most plasma kinetic theory is classical, collisionless and long-range, with self-consistent Vlasov fields.

name: Helicons and Alfven waves in metals
summary: Compensated or uncompensated metals in a strong magnetic field are solid-state plasmas: they carry low-frequency helicon (whistler) waves, observed in sodium, and Alfven waves in bismuth, with dispersion set by carrier density and B exactly as in magnetized plasmas.

name: Plasmons, ion-acoustic waves and phonons in metals
summary: The bulk plasmon of a metal is the Langmuir wave of its electron gas, and longitudinal acoustic phonons in a metal are ion plasma oscillations screened by the electrons, exactly the ion-acoustic wave; Bohm and Staver used this to derive the sound speed of metals.
sources: Bohm & Staver (1951). "Application of Collective Treatment of Electron and Ion Vibrations to Theories of Conductivity and Superconductivity". *Phys. Rev.* 84, 836. [doi:10.1103/PhysRev.84.836](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.84.836)

name: Plasma etching and deposition in chip fabrication
summary: Reactive-ion etching, atomic-layer etching and plasma-enhanced CVD shape every semiconductor device; sheath-accelerated ions give anisotropic etches, and EUV lithography light comes from laser-produced tin plasmas.

name: Debye screening in plasmas and doped semiconductors
summary: Carriers in a non-degenerate semiconductor are a classical plasma: the extrinsic Debye length sets the width of space-charge regions and the screening of ionized donors, and in the degenerate (metallic) limit it becomes the Thomas-Fermi length, both from linearized Poisson-Boltzmann.

name: Dirac fluid: graphene's electron-hole plasma
summary: Near charge neutrality, thermally excited electrons and holes in clean graphene form a strongly interacting two-component relativistic plasma whose hydrodynamic transport violates the Wiedemann-Franz law by more than an order of magnitude.
sources: Crossno et al. (2016). "Observation of the Dirac fluid and the breakdown of the Wiedemann-Franz law in graphene". *Science* 351, 1058. [doi:10.1126/science.aad0343](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aad0343)
